notes: Actual general-fund results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, as reported to the CT Office of Policy and Management, not a budget.

Includes public schools. Connecticut towns pay for schools through the town budget (the board of education and any regional school district), where most other states have separate school districts, so spending and property tax per resident run higher than in those states.
Covers the town's general fund. Water, sewer and other enterprise funds and independent authorities are separate.
Left out: transfers in ($2,735,299) and out ($5,153,336) between the town's own funds and other financing sources such as borrowing, which are not new revenue or spending.

Employee benefits the town records under general government ($191,069, such as health insurance and pensions for town staff) are spread across the town's own departments in proportion to their size, as in other states. Schools and debt service are left out of that spread.
Capital outlay and "other" spending ($25,815,660) are spread across departments in proportion to their size.
The state reports revenue only as property tax, state, federal and all other, so fees, fines and local charges are not shown separately.

Political money counts contributions from PACs, unions, businesses (program-book ads), registered lobbyists and state contractors to City of Torrington's party town committees, filed with the State Elections Enforcement Commission since 2023. Other individual donors ($36,096 in the same period) and party and candidate committees are not counted. Candidates for town office file with the town clerk, so their own committees are not included, and town committees also support state candidates.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Covers the town's general fund. Water, sewer and other enterprise funds and independent authorities are separate.
Left out: transfers in ($0) and out ($2,654,670) between the town's own funds and other financing sources such as borrowing, which are not new revenue or spending.

Employee benefits the town records under general government ($740,139, such as health insurance and pensions for town staff) are spread across the town's own departments in proportion to their size, as in other states. Schools and debt service are left out of that spread.
Capital outlay and "other" spending ($508,621) are spread across departments in proportion to their size.
The state reports revenue only as property tax, state, federal and all other, so fees, fines and local charges are not shown separately.

Political money counts contributions from PACs, unions, businesses (program-book ads), registered lobbyists and state contractors to Town of Washington's party town committees, filed with the State Elections Enforcement Commission since 2023. Other individual donors ($32,086 in the same period) and party and candidate committees are not counted. Candidates for town office file with the town clerk, so their own committees are not included, and town committees also support state candidates.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.
